Gee whiz
JEE WIZ
interjection (Silent Generation slang)
Gee is a softened form of the name Jesus, recorded in American English in the late nineteenth century; gee whiz (also gee whillikins) followed as a longer, playful form. By the 1940s and 50s it was the all-purpose exclamation of wholesome American youth, and gee-whiz even became an adjective for wide-eyed wonder. Few who said it knew whose name it trimmed.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Gee whiz, Dad, can I borrow the car?" There was hardly a more innocent sentence in 1955. Grandparents who said gee whiz meant no harm at all, and most never knew that gee is a shortened form of the name of Jesus. That is exactly why the word is worth a quiet look. The third commandment says, "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). To take a name in vain is to use it emptily, as a noise. The name of Jesus is the highest name there is: God "hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name" (Php 2:9), "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Php 2:10). Jesus Himself told His disciples, "Swear not at all" (Mat 5:34), and James repeats it: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay" (Jas 5:12). A softened form of a holy name is still a use of that name, and the Lord says "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof" (Mat 12:36). None of this is a reason to scold Grandpa. It is a reason for a family to choose its exclamations with love for the name that saves — to say "wow" or "hot diggity" and keep the name of Jesus for prayer and praise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American; gee a softened Jesus, late 19th c.) for a mild exclamation of surprise or wonder — innocently meant, but a minced oath that the third commandment invites us to examine (Exo 20:7).

expand to see more

GEE WHIZ, interj. (American, late 19th c.; staple of the 1940s–50s; also gee, gee whillikins) A mild exclamation of surprise, wonder, or dismay. "Gee whiz, Mom, everybody else gets to go!"

Decode for families: gee is a shortened form of Jesus — Grandpa meant no harm, and we can honour him by choosing a different word.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:7 — "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain."

Php 2:9 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:"

Php 2:10 — "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;"

Mat 5:34 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:"

Jas 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

Modern Corruption

An innocent-sounding exclamation that is, at its root, a softened use of the name of Jesus — a minced oath worth setting aside gently, without scorning those who meant no harm.

expand to see more

The grandparents who said gee whiz were not blaspheming in their hearts; they were using the clean slang of their day, and many chose it precisely to avoid swearing. Their instinct was good. That is why this needs saying gently and without any scorn for them.

Still, a minced oath borrows the sound of a holy name for an everyday noise, and Christ’s name is too precious for that (Php 2:9). The third commandment is not only about cursing; it is about using God’s name lightly. A Christian family can retire gee and gee whiz quietly, explain why to the children, and fill the gap with words that carry no name at all.

Jesus → softened gee (late 19th c. American) → gee whiz, gee whillikins → 1940s–50s all-purpose exclamation.
